Engineering Leadership: The Hard Parts

Juan Pablo Buriticá and James Turnbull

Engineering Leadership: The Hard Parts is about leading engineering teams when the organization around them is chaotic: unclear ownership, shifting priorities, constant crises. The authors met in a breakfast group for startup engineering leaders and kept seeing the same patterns of chaos and dysfunction in organizations of every size. They first turned their approaches into a training course, then into this book (Preface, p. xiii). It is written for new engineering managers, directors and VPs in organizations outgrowing their processes, and staff engineers and architects leading without formal authority (p. xiv). Much leadership advice assumes a stable, well-resourced organization; this book aims to work where that isn't true (pp. xiv–xv).

The book is built on five pillars of leadership — people, mission, plan, process and product — introduced in Chapter 1 and turned into a role description in Chapter 2. Recurring In Practice boxes follow April as she takes over PixelCurl's fractured StudioOps team. Exercises — the Process Pulse survey, the drift diagnostic, the impact-versus-effort mapping session, a technical principles workshop — give leaders something to run the next week.

  • Chapter 6 · pp. 93–122Shipping Products and Code in Chaotic EnvironmentsYou can't do everything, so you must decide what to do and in what order — but elaborate processes in chaos mean serving the process instead of the outcome.▶ simulation

  • Chapter 9 · pp. 173–206Collaborative Technical Practices and Decision MakingIn chaos, success hinges on how well teams work together and decide: decisions must be crisp and fast, with everyone moving the same way.▶ simulation

How the book fits together

The book moves from recognizing chaos and defining your role, through people and direction, to the mechanics of shipping, budgets, technical strategy, collaboration and measurement, before pulling everything together.

The chapter order is the book's; the arrows and the pillar labels are the vault's reading of how the chapters build on each other.

Some threads run through the whole book:

  • Just enough process — light-touch over heavy-handed: the Process Pulse (2), motion over bureaucracy (3), lightweight sprints and estimates (6), RFCs instead of governance boards (9), minimal viable process (11).
  • Focus — clarity as the work: drift and a short list of priorities (5), impact versus effort (6), budgeting as prioritization with dollar signs (7), innovation tokens (8).
  • Psychological safety — from chaos that feels unsafe (3) and team trust (4) to safe disagreement (9), metrics that don't punish people (10), and "without safety, nothing else works" (11).
  • Look after yourself — leaving isn't failure (1), burnout masquerading as resistance (3), and walking away to protect your health (11).

Simulations

Interactive models of the mechanisms the book describes. They are embedded in the lessons too; implementations are the vault’s own.

  • Chapter 2Process pulseRun the book's two-minute Process Pulse survey on three simulated teams, find the one pattern that slows the most people, and try one of the book's two-week experiments.
  • Chapter 3Pilot, medic or engineer?Tell burnout from resistance by its signals, then choose the leadership mode — pilot, medic or engineer — for situations drawn from the book.
  • Chapter 4Team capability checkRate a team on the book's seven observable capabilities, using its own strong and weak examples, and see which one or two to build first.
  • Chapter 5Drift diagnosticTick the signs of drift you see; the book's Table 5-1 gives the likely root causes, one action for this week and the practice that keeps drift away.
  • Chapter 6Impact versus effortPlace the book's example work items and your own on an impact-versus-effort grid and see which quadrant each lands in and what the book says to do with it.
  • Chapter 7Unit economicsSet infrastructure spend, customers, price, other direct costs and customer lifetime, and watch COGS per customer, gross margin and lifetime value move.
  • Chapter 8Innovation tokensBuild April's StudioOps stack from boring and shiny choices with about three innovation tokens to spend, and see whether the tokens go to what differentiates the business.
  • Chapter 9Medium matcherPick a channel for each message — video, audio, chat, email, in person, documentation or a diagram — and compare with the strengths the book gives each medium.
  • Chapter 10Metrics pickerTranslate stakeholder questions into the questions behind them, then build a five-or-six-metric set from the four DORA metrics plus the context metrics for your biggest pain point.

Key concepts

These ideas recur across chapters; each row lists the chapters that discuss them. The definitions are the vault's summaries of the book's explanations.

ConceptDefinitionChapters
Symptoms of chaosTen signs — lack of ownership, no structure, outsized responsibility, undefined process, poor communication, blame, turnover, no strategy, constant crisis, no measurement.1 · 2
Five pillarsPeople, mission, plan, process and product — the parts of an engineering leader's role.1 · 2 · 11
Pockets of stabilityAreas you control and make calm, which can model change for the rest of the organization.1 · 11
Leadership rangeDeliberate switches in tone, pace and focus: diagnose context, thrive in chaos, focus on outcomes, shift between roles.3
Pilot, medic, engineerThree leadership modes: zoom out for direction, stabilize and rebuild trust, or get into the work.3 · 11
Team capabilitiesSeven observable abilities — from turning ambiguity into action to connecting effort to outcomes — that a team builds one or two at a time.4
DriftMotion without meaning: busy from outside, hollowing out the team inside; diagnosed with Table 5-1.5 · 11
Impact versus effortA two-by-two grid for ordering work: quick wins first, big bets broken down, the danger zone avoided.6 · 7
Unit economicsCOGS, CAC, LTV and gross margin — the terms that turn technical decisions into business ones.7
Fully loaded costA person's real cost, typically 1.3–1.8× base salary, plus ramp-up and attrition.7
Build versus buyBuild only what differentiates the business; buy commodity services.7 · 8
Technical principlesA short, team-made set of guides (simplicity first, documentation, testing…) that shape both code and culture.8 · 9 · 11
Innovation tokensDan McKinley's model: about three non-boring technology choices per company — spend them on differentiators.8
RFCs and ADRsRequests for comments decide collaboratively before building; architecture decision records document what was decided.8 · 9
Psychological safetyThe belief you won't be punished for speaking up — the foundation of collaborative decisions and of everything else.3 · 9 · 10 · 11
DORA metricsDeployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore — the starting set, plus one or two context metrics.10 · 11
Goodhart's LawWhen a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure — velocity is the classic case.10
